items.title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices
items.author: Hilke Plassmann, Uma Karmarkar, Vinod Venkatraman
items.content: <article>Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.</article>

items.title: A new view of collectivism
items.author: Thomas Talhelm
items.content: <article>Collectivism is the most widely studied cultural dimension. Yet recent evidence shows that the most-cited scales contain conflicting definitions of collectivism. I review evidence that conceptualizations conflate ‘warm fuzzy’ collectivism and responsibilism. I outline how clarifying the concept can resolve apparent contradictions in previous findings and advance measurement and theory.</article>

items.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
items.author: The Trends Editorial Team
items.content: <article>What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?</article>

items.title: A consonant bias in dogs
items.author: Juan M. Toro
items.content: <article>Do dogs perceive speech similarly to humans? A recent work by Morvai et al. suggests that dogs develop a focus on consonants to identify words, resembling results observed in humans. This is likely the result of massive exposure to language combined with an evolutionarily ancient ability to track regularities in the signal.</article>

items.title: Lost, then found: transient forgetting in humans and machines
items.author: Milan Van Maldegem, Hans Op de Beeck, Niels A. Taatgen, Tinne Tuytelaars, Gido M. van de Ven
items.content: <article>Forgetting can be permanent or transient. An intriguing, recently described form of transient forgetting (TF) in artificial neural networks is the stability gap: a network that has already learned a first task exhibits transient yet substantial forgetting when it begins additional training on a second task alongside the first. Could an analogous phenomenon be found in humans? Following a literature survey, six types of TF in humans were identified, categorised by their sources: learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching, and multitasking. Although all differ in important ways from the stability gap, it is hypothesised that some underlying mechanisms are shared. This opinion article concludes by proposing experiments to test whether a ‘stability gap-like’ form of TF also occurs in humans.</article>

items.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
items.author: Fanny Cazettes, Marieke L. Schölvinck
items.content: <article>For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural–behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.</article>

items.title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self–environment interaction ‘here and now’
items.author: Andrea Serino
items.content: <article>The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body–object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body–object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.</article>

items.title: What can machine learning discover about the nature of emotion?
items.author: Kieran McVeigh, Andrew Smart, Ajay B. Satpute, Karen S. Quigley, Jordan E. Theriault-Brown, Lisa Feldman Barrett
items.content: <article>The science of emotion increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) in the hope of making objective discoveries that resolve century-long debates. We examine research strategies in two main research traditions and show how confirmation bias can arise when theory-based hypotheses are evaluated using theory-laden sampling strategies, model specifications, and inferences. Each tradition manifests its theoretical differences in its ML methods, and, therefore, ML methods cannot settle those differences. The reciprocal relationships between starting assumptions, findings, and conclusions illustrate that ML investigations of emotion, like all scientific investigations, are never free from human experience and beliefs; however, they can be made less biased through a theory-aware research strategy to generate more justified knowledge about emotion.</article>

items.title: Mate preferences and the compatibility puzzle
items.author: Paul W. Eastwick, Amy A.Z. Zhao, Brendan P. Zietsch
items.content: <article>Researchers and laypeople commonly assume that romantic attraction depends, at least in part, on whether potential partners possess the traits that a person says they want. Yet recent studies suggest that such preference-matching effects (Preference × Trait statistical interactions) are often surprisingly small or even absent. Possible psychological explanations include (i) mate choice is multivariate, and so the matching effect for any given trait is heavily constrained, and (ii) traits permit flexible interpretations, in that the same trait can be interpreted differently depending on the partner to whom the trait belongs. Compatibility may derive not mainly from the matching of preferences and traits but rather from the way that two people recurrently extend and build upon shared positive experiences over time.</article>

items.title: Evidence supports constituency-based syntax, movement, and unpronounced elements
items.author: Hiroki Fujita
items.content: <article>Gibson advocates dependency grammar [1], contrasting it with constituency-based accounts that posit movement and phonologically null (unpronounced) syntactic elements [2,3]. Dependency grammar represents sentence structure through word-to-word relations, whereas constituency-based accounts represent sentence structure by grouping words into larger hierarchical constituents. Movement accounts for cases in which a constituent appears in one position but is interpreted in another. For example, in ‘Who did you call?’, ‘Who’ appears sentence-initially but is interpreted as the object of ‘call’; this is analysed as movement from the object position to the sentence-initial position.</article>

items.title: Dependency grammar remains the simplest theory of grammar: a reply to Fujita
items.author: Edward Gibson
items.content: <article>In the original article [1], I claimed that dependency grammar is the simplest theory of grammar. All theories of grammar have rules for connecting words together to make larger units. In dependency grammar, these connections are directly between words. In phrase structure grammars, there is slightly more structure than in dependency grammar, consisting of nonterminal categories for the connected elements, such as the noun phrase and the verb phrase. I argued that these two alternatives are somewhat interchangeable.</article>

items.title: Selection-for-prediction: rethinking early cognitive development
items.author: Stella F. Lourenco
items.content: <article>For decades, core knowledge accounts have proposed that early cognition is organized by innate, domain-specific conceptual or concept-like representations of objects, physical events, number, and agents. I propose a different starting point: infants’ behaviors may arise from domain-general attentional priors—evolutionarily shaped selection biases—interacting with perceptual mechanisms that organize information and support perceptual prediction, rather than from abstract, postperceptual representations. Attentional priors favor ecologically consequential information, including continuity, contact, and synchrony. When such information is disrupted, perceptual prediction error—rather than conceptual contradiction—may produce violation-of-expectation effects. Grounded in constraints on visual input and neural processing, this framework accounts for early successes and systematic failures, suggesting that development begins with perceptual-attentional mechanisms that shape selection, organization, prediction, and learning.</article>
